definition: The heaviest load you can lift once with good form; training loads are set as a percentage of it.
A compound in red cells that makes haemoglobin release oxygen more readily; rises in anaemia and at altitude.

Absolute intensity is the actual workload (watts or pace); relative intensity is that workload as a percentage of a person's own maximum. After training, the same absolute workload is a lower relative intensity.
The gap between the oxygen a hard effort would need and the oxygen actually used, added up over the effort. Used as an estimate of how much energy came from anaerobic sources.
What's left when ATP is spent; its rise is the signal that tells mitochondria to make more ATP.
Stress hormones that rise with hard exercise; adrenaline speeds the breakdown of muscle glycogen. Catecholamines is the group name for adrenaline and noradrenaline.
Making ATP with oxygen from carbohydrate and fat; slower to start but almost unlimited capacity.
A test in which the athlete goes as hard as possible from the start for a set time or until power drops below a cut-off, so power is high early and fades.
The total amount of energy a person can produce without oxygen (from phosphocreatine and glycolysis) before that supply is used up.
The total amount of something (here blood glucose or insulin) over the length of a test, rather than its value at one moment.
The molecule muscles spend for every contraction; it's stored in tiny amounts and must be remade constantly.
An enzyme in the pathway muscle uses to burn fat; its activity is used as a marker of fat-burning capacity.
The highest lactate concentration measured in blood after a hard effort; a rough marker of how much glycolysis was used.
The muscle's capacity to absorb acid; improves with training.
How many small blood vessels surround each fibre; more means faster delivery of oxygen and removal of acid.
Litres of blood the heart pumps per minute = heart rate × stroke volume.
An enzyme found inside mitochondria; how active it is in a muscle sample is used as a marker of how much mitochondria the muscle has.
A test in which the workload is fixed in advance and the rider holds it until they can no longer keep the required cadence.
Participants who do not get the training, so that changes from simply being in the study or the passage of time can be separated from the effect of training.
A number from −1 to 1 describing how closely two measures rise or fall together; 0 means no straight-line relationship.
A vertical jump with a quick dip first; the standard test of lower-body power.
The enzyme that moves phosphate between PCr and ATP.
The thickness of a muscle or fibre; the main driver of how much force it can produce.
The exercise intensity above which carbohydrate supplies more of the body's energy than fat does.
A number calculated from a 50-minute IVGTT that summarises insulin sensitivity; higher is better.
Passive movement of a gas from high to low pressure — how oxygen crosses from air to blood and blood to cell.
Two ways to measure oxygen uptake: collecting expired air in large bags for analysis, or analysing each breath continuously with a metabolic cart.
How big a difference is, independent of whether it's statistically significant; "trivial" means too small to matter.
A straight line linking power output to oxygen use, built from several easier rides and extended upward to estimate the oxygen a supramaximal effort would need.
The set of protein complexes inside mitochondria that use oxygen to make usable energy; their amount is another marker of mitochondrial content.
Calories in minus calories out; fat loss over time requires a sustained deficit.
A tissue removed from the animal and kept alive artificially so it can be measured precisely; precise, but not the same as a living body.
The share of fast-twitch fibres in a small muscle sample removed with a needle, here from the outer thigh (vastus lateralis).
Aerobic exercise done after an overnight fast, before eating.
Burning fat for energy at a given moment; not the same as losing body fat over time.
Fat oxidation is fat burned right now; fat loss is the change in body fat over time, which depends on total energy balance.
How much power falls during an all-out test, from the peak to the minimum, expressed as a percentage of the peak.
A simple exponential recovery — the same fraction restored each minute.
Fat molecules released from fat stores into the blood, where muscles can take them up and burn them.
The liver making new glucose from other molecules, including lactate.
A protein that moves sugar from the blood into muscle cells; more of it helps muscle take up glucose.
The stored form of carbohydrate, kept in muscles and the liver.
Using less stored muscle carbohydrate for the same exercise, usually because another fuel such as fat or blood sugar covers more of the demand.
Breaking glycogen down into glucose units to make ATP fast.
Breaking down carbohydrate without oxygen to make ATP quickly; produces lactate.
The protein in red blood cells that carries almost all the oxygen in blood.
An estimate of insulin resistance worked out from a single fasting blood glucose and insulin value; higher means more resistant.
Fibres containing more than one myosin type (e.g. IIa/IIx); common and intermediate in properties.
Growth in muscle fibre size.
Being short of body water, usually deliberately before a weigh-in.
Oxygen supply inadequate for demand, at the tissue or cell level.
What's released when PCr or ATP is spent; rises during work and is linked to fatigue.
How strongly the body responds to insulin by clearing sugar from the blood; higher sensitivity means less insulin is needed for the same effect.
Acidity inside the muscle fibre; falls (acid rises) with hard work and interferes with energy signalling.
Fat stored inside muscle fibres; a fuel for moderate exercise, especially when fasted.
A test in which sugar is given directly into a vein and blood is sampled repeatedly to see how quickly the body clears it and how much insulin it releases.
An exercise machine that holds cadence at a fixed speed (here 90 rpm) however hard the rider pushes, so only the force and power change.
A labelled version of a molecule, such as a fatty acid or glucose, infused into the blood so researchers can track how fast that fuel is released and used.
The idea (Brooks) that lactate made in one place is carried to another and burned as fuel.
The exercise intensity at which lactate starts building up in the blood faster than the body can clear it.
Thickening of the heart's main pumping chamber; a problem in disease, but proportional growth with body size in athletes is normal.
A genetic condition in which muscle can't break down glycogen; sufferers tire and cramp quickly.
A unit of exercise intensity where 1 MET is the energy used sitting at rest; 'MET-minutes' multiplies intensity by time.
A study that pools the results of many studies to get a more reliable overall answer.
The parts of a cell that use oxygen to produce energy; more of them means muscle can do more aerobic work.
Steady exercise held at a moderate effort for a long block, such as 45 minutes of cycling at about 70% of max heart rate.
Two opposing cell signals: mTOR drives growth; AMPK responds to endurance-type stress and can dampen it.
A small sample of muscle taken with a needle to measure its contents.

alt_definitions.definition: A small piece of muscle (here about 100 mg from the outer thigh) removed with a needle under local anaesthetic for lab analysis.

definition: Maximal voluntary contraction; low-intensity exercise is often set as a % of it.
Growth of the force-producing filaments vs growth of the fluid and non-contractile contents of the fibre; both make muscle bigger, only the first makes it proportionally stronger.
Magnetic-resonance measurement of chemicals (PCr, ATP, glycogen) inside living muscle without a biopsy.
The mitochondrial process that makes ATP using oxygen.
The old idea that extra oxygen breathed after exercise "repays" anaerobic energy; discredited as a measure.
The S-shaped relationship between oxygen pressure and how much haemoglobin is carrying; its shape lets blood load in the lungs and unload in muscle.
The fraction of delivered oxygen that tissues actually take; ~25% at rest for the body, ~60% for the heart.
How long it takes to refill half the spent phosphocreatine after effort — a marker of mitochondrial capacity and a guide to rest intervals.
The angle fibres sit at relative to the line of pull; increases with hypertrophy and raises force at some cost to speed.
Planning training in phases (preparation, competition, transition) that vary volume and intensity.
Ordering training blocks so each one sets up the next (e.g. hypertrophy → strength → power).
A fast backup store that remakes ATP in the first seconds of hard effort; nearly empty after ~10–20 s of all-out work.
Jump-based training that exploits the stretch-shortening cycle.
Cardio done after a protein-only feed (e.g. 25 g whey or casein).
Assigned to groups by chance, which protects against the groups differing in ways the researchers did not measure; this paper says participants were matched and assigned, not randomised.
How fast force rises after a contraction starts; the key quality in explosive lifts, where peak force arrives in a quarter of a second.
Growth concentrated in one part of a muscle, depending on the exercise and range of motion.
The ratio of carbon dioxide breathed out to oxygen taken in; lower values mean more fat is being burned, higher values mean more carbohydrate.
A person's own rating of how hard exercise feels; here on the Borg 6-20 scale, where 13 is 'somewhat hard' and 16 is between 'hard' and 'very hard'.
More in parallel = more force; more in series = more speed and range.
Doing little physical activity; here defined as scoring under 600 MET-minutes per week on a standard activity questionnaire.
A measure of how precisely a group average is known; it is smaller than the spread between individuals, so ± SEM values look tighter than the real person-to-person variation.
How fast a fibre contracts with no load; faster fibres make more power.
A formula that adjusts a weightlifting total for body weight so lifters in different classes can be compared.
A single muscle fibre with its membrane removed so it can be activated and measured in a dish.
Force divided by fibre size; unchanged here, meaning fibres got stronger by getting bigger, not by improving quality.
Short bursts of all-out effort (here 20 seconds) separated by easy recovery; a subset of high-intensity interval training.
A result unlikely to be due to chance alone by the study's chosen threshold (here p < 0.05); it says nothing on its own about how large or important the effect is.
Exercise at an intensity where PCr, pH and oxygen uptake stop drifting — sustainable for long periods.
A fast lengthening of a muscle immediately followed by a powerful shortening — the mechanism of jumping, bounding, and plyometrics.
Blood ejected per heartbeat; the main thing endurance training enlarges.
A fuel the body breaks down for energy, mainly carbohydrate, fat and, to a small extent, protein.
Work at an intensity above the power that produces VO2max, so it cannot be supplied by aerobic metabolism alone and can only be held briefly.
The 'fight or flight' system that ramps up during hard exercise and releases adrenaline and noradrenaline.
A blood marker that tends to fall when training volume rises; used to monitor training stress.
Continuing a set until no more reps are possible.
How fast a fuel such as glucose or fatty acids enters (and leaves) the blood, as opposed to its concentration at one moment.

term: Type II : type I size ratio
definition: How much bigger fast fibres are than slow ones; higher in strength and power athletes.
Two kinds of fast-twitch fibre; IIX are fastest but fatigue quickest, and training tends to convert IIX to IIA.
The most oxygen a person can use per minute during all-out exercise; intensities are often given as a percentage of it.

alt_definitions.definition: The highest rate at which a person can take up and use oxygen during exercise, usually in ml per kg body weight per minute.

definition: The highest rate of oxygen use reached in an all-out exercise test, a standard measure of aerobic fitness, usually given in millilitres per kilogram of body weight per minute.
A standard 30 s all-out cycling test against a fixed resistance set from body weight, used to measure peak and mean anaerobic power.
